name: Unit 4 — AP Psychology — Motivation, Emotion & Personality

cards.back: A need or desire that energizes and directs behavior
Innate, fixed, unlearned behavior patterns triggered by specific stimuli
Physiological needs create drives that push behavior to restore homeostasis
The body’s tendency to maintain a stable internal state
Stomach hormone that signals hunger; think “growlin’ stomach”
Fat-cell hormone that signals fullness and reduces hunger; think “last bite”
Brain structure regulating hunger, thirst, body temperature, and the pituitary gland
Master endocrine gland, directed by the hypothalamus, that releases hormones
Lower physiological needs must be met before higher needs, up to self-actualization
Physiological, safety, love and belonging, esteem, self-actualization
Innate need to form and keep close, meaningful relationships
Motivation to keep an optimal level of alertness, neither too low nor too high
Performance rises with arousal up to an optimal point, then declines
Motivation driven by a need for varied, novel, and intense experiences
Sensation-seeking component: craving intense, exciting, often risky activities
Sensation-seeking component: pursuing new places, experiences, and unusual lifestyles
Sensation-seeking component: seeking stimulation through uninhibited social behavior
Intolerance of repetition and monotony that drives a search for new stimulation
Behavior is pulled by external rewards like money, praise, or grades
Doing something for external rewards or to avoid punishment
Doing something for its own sake, for internal satisfaction
Motivation thrives when needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness are met
Rewarding an already enjoyed activity can reduce intrinsic motivation for it
Desire to challenge oneself and meet a high standard of excellence
Choosing very easy or very hard tasks to avoid responsibility for failure
Explains decision struggles as conflicts between approach and avoidance motives
Choosing between two desirable options
Choosing between two undesirable options
Being both attracted to and repelled by the same option
Choosing between two options that each have appealing and unappealing parts
A response combining bodily arousal, expressive behavior, and conscious experience
The felt experience of emotion or mood
Stimuli or events that trigger an emotional response
Emotion follows awareness of bodily arousal: we fear because we tremble
Bodily arousal and emotional experience happen at the same time, independently
Emotion results from physiological arousal plus a cognitive label for it
Facial expressions can trigger or intensify the matching emotions
Cultural norms for how, when, and where emotions should be expressed
Positive emotions broaden thinking and build lasting resources; negative emotions narrow them
Basic emotions like anger, fear, and happiness recognized across cultures
A person’s characteristic pattern of thinking, feeling, and acting
Freud’s view that unconscious forces, conflicts, and childhood experiences shape personality
Thoughts and information in your immediate awareness
Information outside current awareness that can easily be recalled
Thoughts, feelings, and memories beyond awareness that still influence behavior
Irrational, impulsive part of personality seeking immediate gratification
Rational, planning part of personality that mediates between id, superego, and reality
Moralistic, judgmental, perfectionist part of personality
Ambiguous stimuli used to reveal preconscious and unconscious thoughts
Projective test interpreting what a person sees in ambiguous inkblots
Projective test where people invent stories about ambiguous scenes
Unconscious strategies the ego uses to protect itself from anxiety
Refusing to acknowledge a painful reality
Redirecting impulses from their real source to a safer target
Attributing your own unacceptable feelings or motives to someone else
Inventing logical-sounding excuses that hide the real reasons for behavior
Acting the opposite of an unacceptable impulse or feeling
Retreating to childlike behavior under stress
Unconsciously blocking distressing thoughts and memories from awareness
Channeling unacceptable impulses into socially acceptable, constructive activities
Focuses on the whole person, their uniqueness, and growth toward potential
Accepting and valuing a person without conditions or judgment
Conditions others attach to their approval and positive regard
Innate drive to grow and fulfill one’s full potential
Genuineness, acceptance, and empathy
Personality is learned through observation and shaped by thoughts, behavior, and context
Behavior, personal factors, and environment continually influence each other
Your overall perception and understanding of who you are
Belief in your ability to succeed at a specific task
Your overall emotional judgment of your own worth
Personality is made of stable traits that consistently guide behavior
Openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and emotional stability (neuroticism)
Standardized self-report questionnaires that measure personality traits
Widely used objective personality inventory of hundreds of true-false items
Statistical method finding clusters of related items; revealed the Big Five
Imagination, curiosity, and willingness to try new ideas and experiences
Organization, dependability, discipline, and goal-directed behavior
Sociability, energy, assertiveness, and seeking social stimulation
Warmth, kindness, empathy, cooperation, and trust
Staying calm and resilient under stress; low stability means high neuroticism
